text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co. Tuesday boosted its profile as a supplier of Internet-based systems, launching a sweeping effort to embrace industry partners that often are at odds with each other.
Through a flurry of stepped-up alliances with often warring factions of the industry -- including Oracle Corp. and Microsoft Corp. -- HP said it hopes to offer customers more flexibility.

"Our strategy is to blur the lines," HP Executive Vice President Rick Belluzzo said, adding that the goal was to take advantage of new technologies as they emerge and not to restrict "where good ideas can come from."

Without tying customers to a single technology, HP also said it would help them move from the "creative chaos stage" of the Internet as it exists today, to an environment where companies can manage, measure and control their networks.

Analysts said the strategy enables Hewlett-Packard to catapult itself more broadly into the fast-growing Internet market by extending its reputation for advanced, reliable products combined with leading edge technology from allies.

"It's a time-to-market issue," said Mike Kennedy, vice president of advanced information management at industry consultants Meta Group. "They're not going to get caught in a religious war" over Internet standards.

Kennedy said HP's "compendium strategy" enabled it to tie together a confederation of technology partners and to bill itself as a super-integrator for helping companies build and manage networks based on Internet technology.

The move enables HP, which has worked hard to preserve its entrepreneurial spirit despite being one of Silicon Valley's oldest and most successful firms, to turn the fact that it has not been seen on the Internet's cutting edge into an advantage.

Analysts said many mainstream corporations that have not been leading the push to Internet technologies are expected to be receptive to a major technology company that can provide a level of hand-holding as a systems integrator.
Furthermore, HP is expected to develop a model or template for combining hardware, software and services it can then share with partners also providing integration services.
HP announced an alliance with Actra Business Systems to develop systems for so-called Extranets, Internet-based corporate networks that use the Internet to link up with suppliers and customers.

HP unveiled partnership deals with Oracle, Netscape, Open Market, VeriFone, Visa and Broadvision which will enable it work with those organisations to provide customers critical Internet commerce and security features.
HP said it will develop a NetPC offering, expected by mid 1997, through collaboration with Microsoft, which last month unveiled the standard along with Intel Corp..

The NetPC is expected to go head-to-head next year with a new breed of scaled-down computer terminals called network computers, or NCs, being developed by an alliance that includes Oracle and HP rival Sun Microsystems Inc..
